newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing mayor axed in long delayed reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Beijing mayor axed in long delayed reshuffle.

text.p: The Beijing People's Congress has approved the resignation of Mayor Li Qiyan, the official Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday.
It did not explain why Li, 58, was stepping down, saying only that he would become secretary of the Labour Ministry's Communist Party committee.
The Beijing congress, or city council, also approved Jia Qinglin, 56, the Communist Party chief of southeastern Fujian province, as acting mayor of the nation's capital, Xinhua said.

Chinese sources have said Li stepped down because of his links to Chen Xitong, who resigned as Beijing Communist Party boss in April 1995 after his protege, a vice-mayor, came under investigation for economic crimes and committed suicide.
Chen has since disappeared from public view and has come under investigation for possible wrongdoing.
It was not known if Li was being investigated.
Chen was sacked from the Politburo in September 1995, the most senior official to be ensnared in a corruption scandal since the communists came to power in 1949.
Chinese sources have said Li Qiyan could eventually replace Li Boyong as labour minister. The two men have the same surname but are not related.
The sources said the city government had been virtually paralysed since Chen's downfall and that authorities had decided they could no longer delay naming a new mayor.
The sources also said Jia could be promoted to the post of Beijing Communist Party secretary and capture a seat in the party's powerful Politburo in the run-up to the party's 15th congress next year.

The vice-mayor who committed suicide was found to have used his position to illegally amass 116 houses and build himself a villa on the outskirts of the city. He also masterminded a $37 million embezzlement and graft scam, officials have said.
Corruption was virtually eliminated in the years after the communists came to power in 1949 but has staged a comeback along with economic reforms in the past 17 years.

Communist Party chief and state president Jiang Zemin has declared war on corruption, warning that it was a major threat to the party. Courts frequently impose the death penalty in major corruption cases.
